AlternateTargets: the (截斷眾流) phrase of the (雲門三句)
Senses.Explanation: As a fixed technical term, (截斷眾流句) (139 hits / 69 files) is the middle of the (雲門三句) (Yunmen's three phrases; the set-name itself 76 hits / 44 files): (函蓋乾坤句) (covering heaven and earth) · (截斷眾流句) (cutting off the myriad streams) · (隨波逐浪句) (following the waves). (人天眼目) gives the corpus's own account of the set's origin — (師示眾云)。(函蓋乾坤)。(目機銖兩)。(不涉萬緣)。(作麼生承當)。(眾無對)。(自代云)。(一鏃破三關) (Yunmen's 示眾 with his self-answer 'one arrowhead breaks three barriers'), (後來德山圓明密禪師)。(遂離其語為三句) ('later Deshan Yuanming/Yuanmi separated his words into three phrases'): the scheme is credited not to Yunmen but to his heir (德山緣密) (圓明密禪師 / Deshan Yuanming). In (五燈會元) Deshan Yuanming states them in the first person (有三句語示汝諸人。一句函葢乾坤。一句截斷眾流。一句隨波逐浪。作麼生辯), and later masters recite the set as (雲門三句) (昔日雲門有三句…). The middle phrase became a stock question put to masters across the record — (如何是截斷眾流句) occurs 88 times in 43 files (its companions: 如何是函蓋乾坤句 54 / 33 plus the 函葢 graph 29 / 8; 如何是隨波逐浪句 94 / 46) — each master answering in his own words: (銕蛇橫古路) (人天眼目), (合取狗口) (密雲禪師語錄, J/J10/J10nA158.xml), (無汝開口處) (J/J25/J25nB175.xml), (吞盡不曾乾) (J/J27/J27nB198.xml).
Senses.Note: SenseKey is null: the set is universally called Yunmen's three phrases (雲門三句), but the corpus explicitly says that Deshan Yuanming drew the three-phrase formulation from Yunmen's words. Historical association with Yunmen therefore does not make the meaning master-specific.

Senses.Explanation: The first component means “cut off or sever” (截斷); the second means “the many streams” (眾流). Raw grep: 370 hits across 144 allowlist files (free phrase and 三句 uses together; tag-stripped, 2026-07-11). The texts themselves set it against (隨波逐浪) ('following the waves, chasing the swells'): (截斷眾流) is followed within thirty characters by (隨波逐浪) in 151 places across 66 files, and the reverse order occurs in 59 places across 39 files. The paired wording is the masters' own. (圜悟) (Yuanwu): (若隨波逐浪去)。(種種建立觸處圓融)。(若截斷眾流去)。(把住要津不通凡聖) ('going the follow-the-waves way, every kind of setting-up, everywhere merging; going the cut-off-the-streams way, holding the vital ford, letting neither profane nor holy through'). (宏智) (Hongzhi): (截斷眾流之機)。(則詮表不及)。(且如隨波逐浪底句)。(又作麼生道) ('the working of cutting-off-the-streams cannot be reached by formulation; but the follow-the-waves phrase — how would you say it?').
Senses.Note: Corpus-wide reading; grounded in two independent masters/records (圜悟, 宏智) using the phrase in their own discourse, apart from the Yunmen-three-phrases technical sense.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi's Extensive Record (宏智廣錄), an informal address (小參); the 'cutting off' function cannot be reached by formulation (詮表不及).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'not yet' or 'not there yet' (未在). Across the Chan corpus it is especially frequent as a master's verdict on a reply, shout, verse, or claimed understanding: Zhaozhou says, 'Not there yet; say more' (未在更道); another exchange records, 'You have got it, but you are still not there yet' (你也得只是未在); and an unnamed elder repeatedly waves a visitor away with, 'Not there yet, not there yet; go for now' (未在未在且去). The same words retain their ordinary temporal force in 'Even if you reached a thousand years, you still would not yet be old' (直至千歲也未在). Thus the corpus deploys one literal phrase both as an evaluative reply and in ordinary statements of something not yet reached or completed.
Senses.Note: The exact headword occurs 1,038 times in 230 allowlisted texts. No defining formula of the forms 'the so-called not-there-yet' (所謂未在), 'it is called not-there-yet' (謂之未在 or 名為未在), or 'what is meant by not-there-yet?' (何謂未在) was found. The repeated collocation 'not there yet; say more' (未在更道) occurs 72 times in 39 texts, while 'you have got it, but are still not there yet' (你也得只是未在) and the repeated dismissal 'not there yet, not there yet; go for now' (未在未在且去) display two further recorded shapes. The subject left incomplete is sometimes named, as in 'the matter beyond is not there yet' (向上事未在).

AlternateTargets: the lineage school's claws and fangs
Senses.Explanation: Literally "claws and fangs" (爪牙), here naming equipment displayed in the lineage school's testing exchanges. One record supplies an explicit deployment formula: "one press and one squeeze, one release and one taking-away—the lineage school calls this claws and fangs, and also calls it a handle" (一挨一拶，一縱一奪，宗門中謂之爪牙，亦謂之巴鼻). Elsewhere Huangbo's calling Pei Xiu's name and asking "where are you?" is appraised as use of the lineage school's claws and fangs. Encounters display or conceal them, and later comments appraise whether they are sharp. These passages apply the animal phrase to interview equipment without turning every question into claws and fangs.
Senses.Note: The phrase is not uniformly praise. A passage says various proposed devices each claim to be the lineage school's claws and fangs, then rejects them as still falling within four propositions. Another contrasts two elders who expose their claws and fangs without loss with contemporaries who injure their own edge and hand as soon as they expose them. The corpus itself therefore tests the claim. Family check: "question-and-answer" (問答) names the exchange; "encounter" (機緣) names the recorded encounter or occasion; "probe" (徵) names probing or challenging. This sense names equipment manifested in such exchanges, not every question and not the persons called the school's claws and fangs. The headword has 638 occurrences in 216 allowlisted texts.

Senses.PreferredTarget: teacher epithet: the school's “claws and fangs”
AlternateTargets: teachers called the lineage school's claws and fangs
Senses.Explanation: As a person-denoting epithet, "the lineage school's claws and fangs" (宗門之爪牙) names teachers or heirs rather than equipment they display. A biographical appraisal calls two named teachers the lineage school's claws and fangs and the teaching-cavern's outstanding horns. The praised people are a different referent from an exchange's exposed sharp resources.
Senses.Note: Only one independently anchored person-denoting witness was curated in this pass, so this sense remains provisional. It is retained because the passage directly predicates the epithet of two named teachers, not as another reading of interview equipment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 號稱飽參，寔宗門之爪牙；卓有實行，蓋法窟之頭角。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Biographical praise calls two teachers the lineage school's capable agents, literally its “claws and fangs” (爪牙).

Senses.Explanation: In literal and animal-image passages, "claws and fangs" (爪牙) denotes the claws and fangs of a tiger, lion, or other beast. One address speaks of a sleeping tiger's claws and fangs hidden deep in a cold crag and secluded valley. This concrete anatomy is a different object from the lineage school's sharp resources and from people called its claws and fangs.
Senses.Note: The retained witness is a tiger image in a Chan address. The literal object is split because no single precise gloss can make animal anatomy, exchange equipment, and a person the same referent.
